Letter Quest: Grimm’s Journey Remastered, developed by Bacon Bandit Games and published by Digerati, is a charming and inventive hybrid of word puzzle mechanics and light RPG combat. It takes the foundation of classic word-building games and transforms it into an adventure about a scythe-wielding reaper named Grimm who battles monsters, ghosts, and other quirky enemies not with weapons, but with vocabulary. At first glance, it appears deceptively simple—combine letters on a grid to form words that deal damage to enemies—but as you progress, the game reveals surprising layers of strategy and depth. By merging the analytical thinking of a word puzzle with the resource management and progression systems of an RPG, it creates an experience that is both intellectually stimulating and mechanically satisfying.

The basic gameplay loop revolves around spelling words from a random set of letters to attack enemies. Each tile represents a letter, and longer or more complex words inflict greater damage. High-value letters like Q, Z, or X carry more power but are harder to work into combinations, rewarding creativity and word knowledge. Every encounter functions as a small puzzle in itself, where the player must balance word length, letter positioning, and potential modifiers on the board. The game’s structure is turn-based, so there’s no rush to make a move, but each word you form gives enemies an opportunity to retaliate. This encourages thoughtful decision-making rather than frantic input. As Grimm progresses, new tile effects and enemy abilities are introduced—poisoned letters that harm you if used, cracked tiles that can’t be reused, and special enemies that resist words containing certain letters or lengths. These small variations ensure that each battle feels distinct and that the player is always adjusting their approach.

Between stages, the RPG elements come into play. Gems earned from victories serve as currency that can be used to upgrade Grimm’s health, attack strength, or critical hit chances. There are also books that grant passive bonuses—like increased damage when using certain letters or faster recovery after battle—and weapons with unique properties that can influence your playstyle. The inclusion of these systems transforms what could have been a repetitive word game into something with progression and customization. The shop and upgrade systems give players a reason to revisit earlier levels and grind for better stats, much like a traditional RPG. The sense of forward momentum keeps the game engaging over the long term, and because the difficulty scales gradually, the learning curve remains satisfying without becoming punishing.

The remastered version refines the presentation and performance of the original, offering smoother animations, higher-resolution visuals, and a more responsive interface. The art style is colorful and whimsical, using a cartoonish aesthetic that perfectly complements the game’s humor and lighthearted tone. Grimm and his foes are drawn with exaggerated expressions, and the world he explores feels bright and approachable, even when filled with spooky enemies. The remastered edition also features an improved soundtrack that adds charm to the experience, alternating between playful tunes during exploration and more energetic tracks during combat. Small touches—like the popping animation when a monster explodes in a burst of defeated letters—make the experience feel polished and cohesive. The overall atmosphere is one of cozy challenge, a balance between intellectual engagement and cheerful simplicity.

Despite its friendliness, Letter Quest is not without challenge. As you progress through the campaign, new gameplay modifiers increase the difficulty of previously completed levels. Enemies gain more health, letters become more restricted, and status effects stack in ways that demand more strategic thinking. You’ll often find yourself pausing to consider whether to use a weaker word to conserve better letters for later or to risk everything on a high-damage play. This constant balance of short-term gain versus long-term resource management gives the game a surprising amount of depth. Additionally, each level can be replayed under different conditions—such as timed runs or harder versions of enemies—allowing for significant replayability. For completionists, there are stars to earn, achievements to unlock, and endless modes that test endurance and vocabulary skill.

What keeps the game engaging over time is its variety of mechanics and steady progression. There’s a tangible sense of growth as you acquire new upgrades and become better at spotting high-value words under pressure. The addition of books and special equipment provides minor but meaningful tweaks to your strategy, giving the game a sense of personalization. Still, the repetition inherent in its structure may wear on some players after extended play sessions. The core mechanics don’t evolve drastically beyond the introduction of new modifiers, and the reliance on replaying earlier levels to earn gems can feel grindy. Yet, much like other casual strategy or puzzle games, its charm lies in the rhythm of steady improvement rather than in constant reinvention.

Letter Quest: Grimm’s Journey Remastered also stands out for its accessibility. It’s a game that can appeal to a wide range of players—those who love word puzzles, fans of RPG progression systems, and even younger audiences learning to spell and think strategically. Its design never punishes players harshly for mistakes, and the option to take as much time as needed on each turn makes it relaxing rather than stressful. It’s equally well-suited for short bursts of play or longer sessions, offering just enough structure and reward to keep you coming back. The combination of word-building and RPG elements feels seamless, as though the two genres were always meant to complement one another.

In the end, Letter Quest: Grimm’s Journey Remastered succeeds not because of complexity, but because of clarity. It takes two familiar forms of gameplay—puzzle-solving and leveling up—and fuses them into something fresh, funny, and unexpectedly strategic. Its cheerful presentation and clever design make it easy to underestimate, but behind the adorable visuals lies a game that rewards intelligence, patience, and creativity. It’s the kind of title that manages to be educational without feeling didactic, challenging without being punishing, and nostalgic without being dated. For those looking for a game that engages both vocabulary and imagination, Letter Quest stands as a delightful example of how simplicity, when executed with care and humor, can lead to something genuinely memorable.

I played Letter Quest a lot. More than most people, judging by the achievements. As I'm writing this, I can see them glimmering gold in the background. With that in mind, you might wonder why my review is red and why I spent so much time in the game if I didn't like it.

The answer is simply this: It's not that Letter Quest isn't fun, necessarily, but that it isn't fun enough to actually feel worth it to play. It reminds me of Wordle, a game to fill up space in one's day and then forget about until you're bored again. That's not always a bad thing, but after thinking about it a while I concluded that it's not enough for me. Games as a distraction are different from games as a hobby, and from a Steam game, I expect the latter, not the former.

It doesn't help that the game doesn't have anything close to the full dictionary in it. English isn't my native language, and yet I found myself time and time again spelling out a word only for it to be denied by the game. And yes, I started checking after the third time it happened, and I didn't misspell. For a game where the largest component is coming up with words, it's more than a little lame that you're not allowed to use your full vocabulary.

On a positive note, the game does throw out some conditional puzzle elements. Sometimes you have to use corner letters, sometimes include a certain number of vowels (two, it's always two) or use a minimum or maximum number of letters in your words. This gives the game some legs to stand on, which is good, but let's just say that its gait is more of a hobble than a run. But at least the challenge is there, so if that's what you want from your spelling games, that's another positive.

My conclusion is that this game bored me. Even when using it as a game to play while listening to podcasts, I didn't really look forward to launching it and it's with some relief that I finished it. That's not what one should feel after beating a game. So no, I don't recommend Letter Quest. I'm sure there are better word games out there.

Letter Quest is a game that seems to take heavy influence from the classic Popcap game "Bookworm Adventures", albeit with more RPG elements. As the current #1 Expert Any% speedrun record holder and a former top 10 Bookworm speedrunner, there are several unique perspectives that I think are worth mentioning:

GAMEPLAY
=-=-=-=-=-=-=

I personally really like the gameplay. It's very fun to spell words, and slowly building up your power through the gem upgrades to match your playstyle is extremely rewarding (some upgrades are much more powerful than others, though). I especially love the gem piles at the end of each level, since they are a small extra bonus that rewards skill and thinking things through. It's just a big enough bonus where it feels worthwhile, without the pressure of feeling required to shuffle until you find a big enough word for a good reward.

Similarly, I really like the shops that appear in the middle of levels, since they reward tactical decision making with powerups and give the user a definite choice. I do feel like you could do more with the hangman-esque puzzles (like say, having a higher reward for fewer wrong guesses), but it's a fun break, and is an additional bonus for people who want to go for it.

I wish there were more variety in enemies and attacks, though. Currently, there's only a handful of enemies (with different difficulty tiers, which I personally find super cool), and fighting them gets repetitive quite fast. The various side levels and the challenge modes of levels helps to alleviate this, but the small pool of enemies is a pretty massive flaw with the game. But there's still, a bigger issue:


RNG
=-=-=-=-=-=-=
The game is about spelling letters, and thus you're necessarily dependent on whatever letters you get. But one thing this game suffers from is that you can get completely steamrolled with bad letters far far too easily. There have been many times where I spell a word, and I get over four of one same tile in return, or have one, two, or even ZERO vowels reappear in the new board, and I'm forced to lose a turn shuffling the board through no fault of my own. On occasion, it's just bad luck, but when it happens multiple times per stage, it is just frustrating. Compound this with tile effects that severely limit or remove possible tiles from play without spamming purify potions, and you very often need to shuffle and lose a turn, or even just die, simply because you got moderately unlucky.

This is especially infuriating because when you shuffle, you lose all the gems on the board. Gems give boosts for three turns, and some of them are way way way better than others. The difference between the best gems and the worst ones is either dying on the second enemy or finishing the stage with full health. And once again, when you get gems, and whether they are good or not is entirely random. So if you play the same stage repeatedly, even if all the words you spell and tiles you get are the same, the gems you get radically change the actual outcome you get, completely outside of your control.

All this compounds in certain stages where you need very specific types of words to actually deal an appreciable amount of damage. For example, the final boss takes 5x damage from words containing E and S, and their health bar is increased in accordance with this bonus. But the resulting gameplay is: "Frantically shuffle over and over until you get a board that actually deals damage, and pray you get defensive gems so that you dont die". This is an exceedingly annoying experience.

So overall, while the RNG is fine if you are only playing extremely casually, if you try to do well in the game in the slightest, it becomes an absolute *nightmare*. And even casually, there are many times where you feel completely at the mercy of randomness.


CONCLUSION

If you love word games this is one with a difference! You get to attack & kill monsters & bosses by spelling words. A bit like scrabble, usually the longer the word the better & the harder to use letters (z, q, j, k) equates to more damage done etc. But never fear as there were plenty where you were restricted to using 5 or less letter words & at times only having half the alphabet to work with!

I really enjoyed 100%ing this little gem & my only complaint was that the dictionary of words that the game would accept as valid was a very hit & miss affair. The game also has both a story mode as well as an endless mode, each coming with their own achieves.

I paid $1.50 for this during the summer sale which also included the original Letter Quest: Grimm's Journey (2014). So 2 games means that this was excellent value! I do highly recommend this especially if you manage to get it on sale like I did. A great lil gem & I shall enjoy 100%ing the original in the future that it came with.

Continuing on with my love of typing games, I stumbled upon Letter Quest. Typing of the Dead still (to this review, anyway) holds the title for the best typing game I've played, dare I say, better than All The Right Type. If you're looking to improve your vocabulary or challenge younger nephews with an RPG typing game, should be up your alley.

The [b]gameplay[/b] is quite straightforward and simple. Mouse and keyboard rules; mostly mouse to select and keyboard to type. Don't be fooled by how the graphics look, this game will challenge the depths of the human dictionary. There were occasions I had to test Google as well. The progressions themselves are nothing to laugh at. The boss levels will have absurd (however, welcomed) challenges. One boss I came across would only take damage if I started the word with a vowel. Another boss would only take damage if I had a minimum four letter word. Sounds straight forward right? Well, when you're given a certain amount of letters it becomes a challenge. There is an option to shuffle, it does skip the player's current term, and usually results in damage. There are power-ups available in the game for the player to acquire as they gain more cash. 

The [b]graphics and visuals[/b] are appropriate to the game. User interface is especially friendly and easy to navigate. The animations are well done and seems like a solid effort was put it. The attacks, damage, and even skins are pretty neat. The [b]sounds and music[/b] are okay. I'm not sure what sort of demands would be put in this category, but some sort of hardcore thor nordic rock or some random-ness may have upped this domain. None the less, nothing to complain about!

Overall, the game is good in my opinion and is worth a purchase on sale if it's something you're interested in. Is it like a game of Boggle? Sure, but it's got little systems of rewards and animations that make it fun when you're friends are too busy to play Boggle. I wish it would up the difficulty a little more gradually, it can get pretty hard pretty fast.
